confidence_rationale: The highest mapping-fidelity entry in this pull because it is at REE's own level of description: a computational formalism (Bayesian inverse planning) for inferring another agent's goal by inverting a model of rational planning. It supplies MECH-129 the obstruction-detection computation (an inferred goal + a rationality model lets you score whether a trajectory serves or defeats the goal) and MECH-164 component 1 (agent-indexed terrain inference: infer what the other is inferring/pursuing). Held at 0.7 because the validating experiments are simple 2D maze stimuli with human goal-inference as the criterion, so it proves the computation is humanlike in a toy domain, not that it scales to REE's multiagent terrain.
failure_signatures: Inverse planning recovers goals well only when the observer's generative model of the agent's planning is approximately correct; under model mismatch (the other plans differently than assumed) goal inference degrades -- a REE agent-indexed terrain inference inherits this and can mis-infer the other's goal/harm gradients, which RHM-5 flags as the 'badly-inferred terrain' that must NOT be weighted self-like.

The framework infers goals from fully-observed action in small discrete state spaces; it does not address the cost of the inference at scale or partial observability of the other's state -- both load-bearing for a deployable MECH-164 substrate.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Human action understanding can be modelled as Bayesian inverse planning: observers infer the goals (and other mental states) behind an agent's behaviour by inverting a model of approximately-rational planning, integrating the likelihood of observed actions with a prior over goals. Three maze experiments show this predicts human goal inferences quantitatively.
mapping.ree_translation: Both MECH-129 and MECH-164 require inferring another agent's goal structure from their behaviour. Inverse planning is the precise computational instantiation of that inference. For MECH-129 it grounds the goal-interference signal: with an inferred goal and a rational-planning model you can score whether your trajectory raises the cost of the other's plan (obstruction). For MECH-164 it grounds component 1 (agent-indexed terrain instantiation): inferring 'what another agent would be inferring about the terrain (their goal and harm gradients)' IS inverting their planner over the residue field, indexed to them rather than to self.
mapping.mapping_caveat: Baker et al. validate against human goal inferences in small 2D mazes with fully-observed actions; the model is a normative/descriptive account, not a claim about the brain's implementation, and says nothing about self-like WEIGHTING of the recovered goals into one's own value function (MECH-164 component 2) -- only about recovering them (component 1). The transfer to a multiagent REE terrain with partial observability and the cost of inference at scale is untested here.
mapping.source_context: Computational cognitive science; human psychophysics with animated agents navigating simple mazes

confidence_components.notes: Foundational, highly-cited computational ToM. Mapping fidelity is the highest in the set because the paper operates at REE's level (a computation over goals), directly instantiating MECH-164 component 1 and MECH-129's goal-inference substrate. Transfer risk moderate: toy maze validation, no scaling/partial-observability story, and it covers goal RECOVERY not self-like weighting.
